spots.name: St Dunstan-in-the-East Church Garden
spots.blurb: A bombed-out medieval church with a Wren tower whose roofless nave has been taken over by ivy, fig trees and climbing vines, with a small fountain in the middle and benches tucked into the arches. Office workers eat lunch here in near silence; early on a weekday morning it is often nearly empty and works well with a coffee and a book. It sits on a steep side street between London Bridge and the Tower, so most people walk straight past.
spots.tips: Come before 9am or after 5pm on a weekday; lunchtime and sunny weekends bring photographers. Enter from St Dunstan's Hill or Idol Lane; the benches under the arches get the most morning sun.

spots.name: Postman's Park
spots.blurb: A pocket park behind St Paul's, once a lunch spot for workers from the old General Post Office next door, with a covered loggia holding the Watts Memorial: rows of Victorian ceramic tiles honouring ordinary people who died saving others. It is shaded, hushed and contemplative, the kind of place people come to sit alone for twenty minutes. Benches sit around a small pond and mature plane trees keep it cool in summer.
spots.tips: Enter from King Edward Street or Little Britain; the benches under the loggia stay dry in light rain. Weekday 12-2pm is the only time it fills up.

spots.name: The Garden at 120
spots.blurb: One of the City's largest free public roof gardens, fifteen storeys up on top of Fen Court, with wisteria pergolas, fruit trees, a long shallow rill and wide views of the Gherkin, the Shard, Tower Bridge and the river. Unlike Sky Garden there is no booking and no bar pressure: you take the lift up, find a bench and stay as long as you like. On summer weekday evenings it has stayed open into the evening, which makes it one of the calmest free places in the City to watch the light go.
spots.tips: Enter via the Fenchurch Street lobby and expect a bag check and a short queue at lunchtime; late afternoon on a weekday is usually near-empty. Weekend hours are shorter and it shuts on bank holidays; confirm the day's closing time on the official site before planning a sunset visit.
spots.hours: Mon-Fri approx 10am-9pm in summer and 10am-6:30pm in winter; Sat-Sun approx 10am-5pm; closed bank holidays (check site)

spots.name: Cloister Garden, Museum of the Order of St John
spots.blurb: A small walled garden in a monastic style beside the Priory Church of the Order of St John, just off St John's Square, with a fountain, medicinal and herb planting and benches in the shade. It is almost completely silent apart from the water, and even Clerkenwell locals often do not know it is open to the public. Good for an hour of reading with nobody around.
spots.tips: Walk through the passage beside the Priory Church on St John's Square, opposite St John's Gate. The garden follows the museum's opening days and occasionally closes for events, so check the museum site before a special trip. Bring your own coffee.
spots.hours: During museum opening hours only (recently around Wed-Sat 10am-5pm; days vary, check site)

spots.name: Wellcome Collection Reading Room
spots.blurb: A hybrid library-gallery on level 2 of the free Wellcome Collection museum, with sofas, cushions, a wide staircase to sit on, and shelves you can browse without a card or a booking. Students from nearby UCL treat it as a common room, but it rarely feels crowded. Rainy afternoons here with a book are as low-key as central London gets.
spots.tips: Take the stairs past the cafe to level 2; the window seats go first. The Wellcome Library next door has proper desks if you need to work (free membership, bring ID). Closed Mondays.
spots.hours: Tue-Sun 10am-6pm; closed Mon (museum opens late on Thu; check site for Reading Room times)

spots.name: Brown Hart Gardens
spots.blurb: A raised Edwardian stone terrace built on top of the Duke Street electricity substation, a short walk south of Oxford Street, with planters, benches and a small cafe. Most shoppers never look up, so it stays surprisingly quiet even on Saturdays. You sit above the street noise and watch Mayfair go by from a stone balustrade.
spots.tips: Climb the steps from Duke Street or Brown Hart Gardens; the benches on the south side catch afternoon sun. The gates are locked in the evening.
spots.hours: Daily approx 8am-8pm (shorter in winter; cafe daytime only)

spots.name: Royal Festival Hall foyers and riverside terrace
spots.blurb: Since 1983 the Grade I-listed Royal Festival Hall has kept an open-foyer policy: anyone can walk in, take a table on the upper levels, plug in a laptop, doze in a chair or read for hours with no ticket and no purchase. Upstairs the river-facing balconies look straight across the Thames at Westminster and the Embankment lights. The riverside walk outside is lit and busy until late, so it is a rare central spot that works both wet and late.
spots.tips: Level 5 has the quietest tables and good river views, and the National Poetry Library up there is free to browse. Bringing your own food and soft drinks into the foyers is allowed; avoid the pre-concert rush around 6-7:30pm.
spots.hours: Building daily approx 10am-11pm (check site); riverside walk 24h

spots.name: Parliament Hill viewpoint
spots.blurb: The grassy summit in the south-east corner of Hampstead Heath, about 98m up, with a protected panorama of the skyline from St Paul's to the Shard and Canary Wharf. Locals bring a blanket at dusk and sit in a loose, friendly crowd of picnickers and dog-walkers; at dawn it is nearly empty and the city glows below. It is famous, but big and open enough that it never feels like a queue.
spots.tips: Walk up from Gospel Oak Overground (about 10 min); the bench-lined crest faces south-east, so sunrise is the truly quiet slot. There is no lighting on the Heath, so head back down towards Highgate Road or Gospel Oak once the sky goes dark.

spots.name: The Hill Garden and Pergola
spots.blurb: An Edwardian raised walkway of weathered stone columns draped in wisteria, vines and roses, built for Lord Leverhulme above West Heath and now gently going back to nature. It looks over a formal terraced garden with a lily pond and out across the trees, and on a weekday morning you can wander most of the long colonnade alone. It feels like a film set that nobody bothered to fence off.
spots.tips: Enter via Inverforth Close off North End Way (Golders Green or Hampstead tube, then about a 15-min walk); the western end of the pergola looks over West Heath. Weekend afternoons draw photo shoots, so go early.
spots.hours: 8:30am to around dusk (closing time varies by month; check City of London site)

spots.name: Parkland Walk
spots.blurb: London's longest local nature reserve runs along a disused railway cutting from Finsbury Park up to Highgate, past the old platforms at Crouch End, graffiti-covered bridges and a spriggan sculpture peering from an arch. It is shaded, mostly free of traffic noise and used by local runners, dog-walkers and people who just want a slow half-hour under the trees. It came up in City Hall's survey of Londoners' favourite hidden gems.
spots.tips: Start at the Oxford Road entrance by Finsbury Park and walk north; the old Crouch End platforms are the best spot to sit. The path is unlit and can be muddy after rain, so treat it as a daytime place.

spots.name: Dalston Eastern Curve Garden
spots.blurb: A community garden built on a disused railway curve behind Dalston Junction, with wood-chip paths, a pizza oven, a small cafe-bar serving coffee and drinks, and paper lanterns strung through the trees after dark. It is free to enter and locals come to read on the benches by day or sit under the lights with a drink in the evening. It feels like someone's back garden rather than a venue.
spots.tips: The entrance is a gap in the wall at 13 Dalston Lane, near Dalston Junction Overground. Summer evenings are lantern-lit and run late; winter closing is around dusk. The covered Pineapple House has a wood-burning stove for cold or wet evenings.
spots.hours: Daily; seasonal, roughly late morning to dusk in winter and to 9-10pm on summer evenings (check site)

spots.name: The Tide, Greenwich Peninsula
spots.blurb: A raised linear park beside the O2 designed by the studio behind New York's High Line, with wooden lounge benches, sculptures and a run of quieter seating above the Thames. From the riverside stretch the view runs across the water towards Canary Wharf, so on many evenings the sun goes down behind the towers before the lights come on. It is lit, managed and mostly used by residents rather than visitors.
spots.tips: From North Greenwich tube walk through Peninsula Square past the Design District and follow the raised path towards the cable car; the benches at the riverside end are best for sunset. Bring a layer, it is exposed and windy.
spots.hours: Open daily as part of the estate's public realm; no gate hours published, so treat it as an early-to-evening spot

spots.name: Stave Hill
spots.blurb: A 9m artificial mound built from old dock rubble in the middle of Russia Dock Woodland, with steps up to a flat top holding a bronze relief map of the vanished Surrey Docks. From the platform you get a wide view of Canary Wharf across the river, the City to the west and the Shard, with almost nobody else up there. It is genuinely a locals-only spot inside a quiet residential peninsula.
spots.tips: Nearest stations are Canada Water or Rotherhithe; enter the woodland from Timber Pond Road or Salter Road and follow signs. Sunset over the City is the moment; it is unlit, so come down before it gets fully dark.
